title: When outcomes are equally likely
objectives: Compute a probability by counting, and check that the outcomes really are equally likely.
Spot an argument that counts unequal outcomes as equal.

screens.prose: Roll two fair dice and record the total. There are 11 possible totals, from 2 to 12. Predict which comes up most, then run the rolls.

state.caption: Run some rolls and watch the bars.

screens.question: After 1,000 rolls, which total comes up most often?

options.why: A total of 2 needs a 1 on both dice. Only one roll does that.
A total of 12 needs a 6 on both dice. Only one roll does that.
You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. Run 1,000 rolls and compare the 2 bar with the 7 bar.

hints.text: Run 1,000 rolls and look for the tallest bar.
Compare these end bars with the bars in the middle.

feedback.correct: 7 comes up about six times as often as 2 or 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 rolls and find the tallest bar.

explain.text: The 7 bar towers over the 2 and 12 bars. So the 11 totals are not equally likely, and $\tfrac{1}{11}$ each would be wrong. Next we see why.

screens.prose: Here is why. Each cell is one of the 36 rolls, and every roll is equally likely. The number in a cell is that roll's total.
screens.question: Shade every roll with a total of 10.

hints.text: Which pairs of faces add to 10?
Tens sit on one short diagonal at the bottom right.
4 and 6, 5 and 5, 6 and 4. That is three cells.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find every cell that shows 10.

byKey.r6c4: You missed (6, 4). Red 6 with blue 4 differs from red 4 with blue 6.
byKey.r5c5: You missed (5, 5). A double is one roll, and it counts.
byKey.no-double: You missed (5, 5). A double is one roll, and it counts.
byKey.one-order: You missed (6, 4). Red 6 with blue 4 differs from red 4 with blue 6.
byKey.one-order-b: You missed (4, 6). Red 4 with blue 6 differs from red 6 with blue 4.

explain.text: Three rolls total 10, but six total 7 and only one totals 2. Each total is a group of rolls, and the groups differ in size. That is why the 7 bar was tallest.

screens.prose: The 36 rolls are **equally likely outcomes**: each has chance $\tfrac{1}{36}$. Then the chance of an event is a count: $$P(E) = \frac{|E|}{|S|}.$$ The chart groups the 36 rolls by total.

state.caption: 36 equally likely rolls, grouped by total

screens.question: What is $P(\text{total is } 7)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: P(total is 7)
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{6}$, or 0.1667 to 4 places.

hints.text: How many of the 36 rolls total 7?
Read the height of the 7 bar.
Six rolls total 7, out of 36.

feedback.correct: Six of the 36 equally likely rolls: $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rolls in the event, then divide by the 36 rolls in $S$.

byKey.eleven: You divided by the 11 totals. They are not equally likely, so count rolls, not totals.
byKey.half: You split into 7 and not 7. Those two are not equally likely: 6 rolls against 30.
byKey.seven: You used the total itself as the count. Six rolls total 7.
byKey.one: That is the chance of one particular roll, such as (3, 4). Six rolls total 7.

explain.text: You counted 6 rolls in the event and 36 in $S$: $P = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$. Counting works here because every roll has the same chance.

screens.prose: A bet pays out when the total is 10 or more.

state.caption: 36 equally likely rolls, grouped by total

screens.question: What is $P(\text{total} \ge 10)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Which totals count, and how many rolls give each?
Add the heights of these three bars.
$3 + 2 + 1 = 6$ rolls out of 36.

feedback.correct: Six rolls: three for 10, two for 11, one for 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the rolls behind 10, 11 and 12, then divide by 36.

byKey.totals: You took 3 of the 11 totals. Totals are not equally likely; count the rolls behind each.
byKey.one-each: You gave each total one roll. 10 has three rolls, 11 has two, and 12 has one.

explain.text: You added the rolls behind each total: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$. So $P(\text{total} \ge 10) = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$, the same as a 7.

screens.prose: A bent coin lands heads with chance 0.6. Its sample space is still $\{\text{H}, \text{T}\}$: two outcomes.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{H})$, and where does it come from?

options.why: You counted outcomes. That works only when they are equally likely, and this coin favours heads.

options.text: 0.6, from the coin itself. H and T are not equally likely, so counting does not apply.
Either 0.6 or $\tfrac{1}{2}$, depending on the method.
options.why: An event has one chance. Counting gives $\tfrac{1}{2}$ only by wrongly treating H and T as equal.

options.text: It cannot be known, since the outcomes are not equally likely.
options.why: Unequal outcomes still have chances. We cannot get them by counting, but here we are told 0.6.

hints.text: What does $\tfrac{|E|}{|S|}$ assume about the outcomes?
Compare the two bars.
Counting needs every outcome to have the same chance. These two do not.

feedback.correct: Counting needs equal chances, and this coin has none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether H and T are equally likely before you count.

explain.text: $\tfrac{|E|}{|S|}$ would give $\tfrac{1}{2}$, which is wrong for this coin. The rule needs equally likely outcomes, and H and T are not. The 0.6 comes from the coin, by measuring it or by being told.

screens.prose: Alex argues: “Either the total is 7 or it is not. That is two outcomes, so $P(7) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.”
screens.question: What is wrong with Alex's argument?

options.text: Nothing: two outcomes, one of them a 7, so $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
options.why: You accepted two outcomes as equally likely without checking. The grid shows 6 rolls for 7 and 30 against.

options.text: He should use the 11 totals, so $P(7) = \tfrac{1}{11}$.
options.why: That swaps one unequal list for another. The 11 totals are no more equally likely than “7” and “not 7”.

options.text: His two outcomes are not equally likely: 6 rolls give 7 and 30 do not.
“Not 7” is not an outcome, so it cannot be counted.
options.why: “Not 7” is a fine event. The trouble is that it holds 30 rolls, not 1.

hints.text: Count the rolls behind each of Alex's two outcomes.
These are the rolls that total 7.
Six rolls total 7 and the other 30 do not. Chances of $\tfrac{6}{36}$ and $\tfrac{30}{36}$ are not a 50:50 split.

feedback.correct: One side holds 6 rolls, the other 30.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many rolls sit behind “7” and behind “not 7”.

byKey.nothing: You accepted two outcomes as equally likely without checking. The grid shows 6 rolls for 7 and 30 against.

explain.text: Alex split $S$ into two events, but one holds 6 rolls and the other 30. Counting outcomes gives a chance only when they are equally likely. Here $P(7) = \tfrac{6}{36}$ and $P(\text{not } 7) = \tfrac{30}{36}$.

screens.prose: You counted rolls and divided by 36. Why does that work? Suppose $S$ has $n$ equally likely outcomes, and $E$ holds $k$ of them.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Every outcome has the same chance; call it $c$.
The $n$ chances add up to $P(S) = 1$, so $nc = 1$.

hints.text: Start by naming the common chance.
All the outcomes together make up $S$, and $P(S) = 1$.
Name $c$, use $P(S) = 1$ to find it, then add up $k$ copies of it.

feedback.correct: Equal chances that add to 1 must each be $\tfrac{1}{n}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of one outcome before the chance of $E$.

explain.text: Equal chances that add to 1 must each be $\tfrac{1}{n}$, and $E$ collects $k$ of them. If the chances differ, the first line fails, and so does the count. That is why Alex's $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and the bent coin go wrong.

screens.prose: A trader says: “Each day the index goes up or down. Two outcomes, so $P(\text{up}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.” Her log of 10 days reads U U D U D U U D U D.
screens.question: What is the best response?

options.text: She is right: two outcomes, so $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
options.why: You counted outcomes without checking they are equally likely. Indices often rise on more days than they fall.
Ten days is a small sample. 0.6 is an estimate, and another ten days could give 0.4 or 0.8.

options.text: Up and down need not be equally likely. The log suggests about 0.6, so counting cannot justify $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Add a third outcome, flat, so $P(\text{up}) = \tfrac{1}{3}$.
options.why: Adding flat does not fix it. Three outcomes are no more equally likely than two.

hints.text: Count the up days in the log.
Six of the ten days were up.
Counting needs equally likely outcomes, and nothing says up and down are. Measure the chance instead.

feedback.correct: Measure the chance; do not count it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether up and down are equally likely before you count.

explain.text: Counting gives $\tfrac{1}{2}$ only if up and down are equally likely, and nothing guarantees that. The log's 6 up days in 10 estimates about 0.6. A longer log would pin it down better.

screens.prose: A bet on two fair dice pays £10 if the red die beats the blue die, and nothing otherwise. Its fair price is what it pays on average per roll.
screens.question: What is the fair price to play once, in pounds?

hints.text: Red beats blue and blue beats red are mirror images. How many ties are there?
The diagonal holds the ties.
$36 - 6 = 30$ rolls have a winner, and half of them have red higher: 15. Over 36 rolls the bet pays $15 \times \text{£}10$.

feedback.correct: £150 over 36 rolls is about £4.17 a roll.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rolls where red wins, then share the total payout over all 36.

byKey.half: You split the rolls into win and lose. The 6 ties pay nothing, so red wins only 15 of 36.
byKey.third: You treated win, lose and tie as equally likely. Ties hold 6 rolls, while wins and losses hold 15 each.
byKey.all: That is the payout, not its average. The bet pays on only 15 of the 36 rolls.

explain.text: Swapping the dice turns each red win into a blue win, so both hold the same number of rolls. With 6 ties, each holds $\tfrac{36 - 6}{2} = 15$. The fair price is $\text{£}10 \times \tfrac{15}{36} \approx \text{£}4.17$.

ideas: With equally likely outcomes, a chance is a count: $P(E) = \tfrac{|E|}{|S|}$.
Check the outcomes first. The 36 rolls are equally likely; the 11 totals, and “7 or not 7”, are not.
When outcomes are unequal, such as a bent coin or an index, the chance must be measured, not counted.

formula.name: Equally likely outcomes
formula.note: Only when every outcome in $S$ has the same chance, $\tfrac{1}{|S|}$.

summary.trap: “It happens or it does not, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.” Two outcomes are not a 50:50 split unless they are equally likely.

quiz.question: What is $P(\text{total is } 4)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the rolls that total 4, keeping the dice apart.

byKey.eleven: You divided by the 11 totals. They are not equally likely; count rolls.
byKey.one-order: You missed one roll. (1, 3) and (3, 1) are both there, and so is (2, 2).

quiz.prose: Two fair coins are tossed. Kim says the outcomes are no heads, one head and two heads, so one head has chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
quiz.question: What is the chance of exactly one head? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: HT and TH: 2 of 4 equally likely outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the outcomes with the coins kept apart.

byKey.kim: You used Kim's list. One head covers HT and TH, while two heads covers only HH.
byKey.quarter: You counted HT but not TH. Either coin can be the head.

explain.text: Keep the coins apart: HH, HT, TH and TT are equally likely. One head covers HT and TH. So the chance is $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, not Kim's $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

quiz.prose: A bet pays £12 if two fair dice total 7, and nothing otherwise.
quiz.question: What is its fair price, the average payout per roll, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the winning rolls out of 36, then share the payout.

byKey.eleven: You gave 7 a chance of $\tfrac{1}{11}$. The 11 totals are not equally likely.
byKey.half: You split into 7 and not 7. Only 6 of the 36 rolls win.
byKey.one: You counted one winning roll. Six rolls total 7.

explain.text: Six of the 36 rolls win, so over 36 rolls the bet pays $6 \times \text{£}12 = \text{£}72$. Shared over 36 rolls that is £2.00 a roll.

quiz.prose: Counting works only on a list of equally likely outcomes.
quiz.question: Which list is equally likely?

options.text: The number of heads in two fair tosses: 0, 1, 2
options.why: 1 head happens two ways, HT and TH, while 0 and 2 happen one way each.

options.text: The total of two fair dice: 2 to 12
options.why: 7 comes from six rolls and 2 from one. The totals are not equally likely.

options.text: The ordered results of two fair tosses: HH, HT, TH, TT
Tomorrow's move of an index: up or down
options.why: Nothing makes up and down equally likely. That chance has to be measured.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the list where no item hides several ways of happening.

explain.text: HH, HT, TH and TT each have chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. The other lists group outcomes unevenly, or have chances that nothing forces to be equal.
